description_full: Sandisk Corporation develops, manufactures, and sells data storage devices and solutions using NAND flash technology in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and internationally. The company provides solid state drives for desktop and notebook PCs, gaming consoles, and set top boxes; and flash-based embedded storage products for mobile phones, tablets, notebook PCs and other portable and wearable devices, automotive applications, Internet of Things, industrial, and connected home applications, as well as removable cards, universal serial bus drives, and wafers and components. It sells its products to computer manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers, datacenters, private cloud customers, cloud service providers, resellers, distributors, and retailers through its sales personnel, dealers, distributors, retailers, and subsidiaries. Sandisk Corporation was incorporated in 2024 and is based in Milpitas, California.

financial_summary: Sandisk Corporation is a large-cap technology business with a $97.2B market cap on $20.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +175% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +79.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 46% against a 10% cost of capital — a 35-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 51% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $11.5B in free cash flow — roughly 57 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.02× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 61% operating margin runs 55pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.62x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 536 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 484% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 54% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 71% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 114% and a beta of 1.19, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $12.8B traded a day.
val: The stock trades 75% below its DCF fair value of $340, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $153 to $784 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 5.5 vs 25.8, EV/EBITDA 4.3 vs 16.6 and P/FCF 8.5 vs 24.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 11.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 13.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $245 on average, 187% above the price.
The price implies 7.4% annual cash-flow growth, 26pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 46% clears the cost of capital of 10.4% by 35pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.86).
It runs a 51% gross margin and converts 57% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.02x.
ROE of 73% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 6.6% of revenue on R&D and 1.1% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $4.8B (5% of market cap).
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
growth: At current returns, reinvesting 33% of profits supports about 15.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 3.0x annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 0.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 38.8% on average.
Analysts expect 25.7% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and institutions hold 77%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (32 sales, net $110.6M sold).
It returns 4.7% a year to shareholders (4.7% in buybacks).
people: With about 11,100 employees, each generates about $1.8M of revenue, 4.8x the Technology median.
That works out to $1.0M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.2M (3x revenue per employee).
